Reading and Discussion

STAT 159: Collaborative and Reproducible Data Science

Reproducible Research Standard (RSS) Framework

Reading

  • Title: The Legal Framework for Reproducible Scientific Research
  • Author: Victoria Stodden
  • Journal: Computing in Science & Engineering
  • Year: 2009
  • https://www.stodden.net/papers/Legal-STODDEN2009.pdf

About

Victoria Stodden proposes the Reproducible Research Standard (RRS).

It aligns intellectual property law with open scientific norms.

Reading’s Key Points

The Legal Conflict

  • Default copyright applies automatically to digital work.
  • Copyright laws grant exclusive monopolies to creators.
  • This legal barrier blocks computational reproducibility.
  • Scientific progress requires continuous modification and reuse.
  • Standard copyright structures run counter to scientific ethos.

The Research Compendium

  • Academic papers are merely advertising for scholarship.
  • True scholarship includes the complete development environment.
  • A full research compendium requires five components:
    • Manuscript source files.
    • Data and collection documentation.
    • Experimental source code scripts.
    • Final figures and processing logs.
    • Auxiliary web presentation materials.

Copyright and Data

  • Raw objective facts cannot be copyrighted.
  • Applying standard copyright to facts is meaningless.
  • Data curation requires immense time and labor.
  • Original dataset selection and arrangement can hold copyright.

The Share Alike Problem

  • Copyleft licenses mandate identical downstream licensing.
  • Share Alike clauses severely restrict open scientific reuse.
  • They block commercial industry from using academic research.
  • They complicate proper author attribution in derivative works.
  • Science needs credit without restrictive licensing bounds.

The Reproducible Research Standard (RRS) Solution

  • The RRS acts as an umbrella licensing algorithm.
  • It separates a compendium into distinct asset categories.
  • It applies specific open frameworks to each asset:
    • Modified BSD for code scripts.
    • Creative Commons BY for media and narrative text.
    • Science Commons Database Protocol for public domain data.
  • It mandates viral attribution for all components.
  • It protects scientists from uncredited intellectual theft.

Share Alike Issues

Why Share Alike Blocks Industry

  • The Forced Open-Source Trap: Companies must open-source their entire product if they use your code.

  • Financial Risk: Corporate legal teams strictly ban engineers from using Share Alike assets.

  • Zero Adoption: Your research gets ignored by industry developers due to legal liability.

  • Kills Tech Transfer: Universities cannot license the technology to commercial startups.

Why Share Alike Hurts Science

  • License Incompatibility: You cannot mix two datasets if they have different Share Alike terms.

  • Attribution Stacking: Combining multiple works makes it impossible to track clean credit.

  • The Instrument Barrier: Academic code often must run inside proprietary software like MATLAB.

  • Scientific Norms: Science prioritizes the spread of truth over forcing specific licenses.

Stodden’s Alternative: “Viral Attribution”

  • Instead of forcing others to share their entire project, Stodden advocates for mandatory credit.

  • If a company uses your academic code, they can keep their product secret, but they must legally cite your paper and give you credit.

  • This satisfies the academic reward system (citations) without killing economic innovation.

Attribution Clause

Attribution Clause

According to Stodden’s framework, a strong attribution clause is not only enough—it is actually the ideal mechanism for scientific compliance.

Here is why Stodden argues that attribution alone is the correct legal tool for open science.

It Aligns with Existing Scientific Norms

The Currency of Science: In academia, the primary reward system is credit, impact, and citation.

Scientists do not usually lose sleep over whether someone made money off their idea; they care if they were plagiarized or left uncredited.

Legal Enforcement of Citations: Traditional academic citation is just a social norm. By using an attribution-only license (like CC BY or modified BSD), you turn a polite scientific etiquette into a legal requirement.

If someone uses your compendium without citing you, they are committing copyright infringement.

“Viral Attribution” Without the “Share Alike” Damage

  • Stodden introduces the concept of viral attribution.
  • This means the license requirement to give credit propagates forward to any downstream work that builds on your research.
  • Unlike Share Alike, it only forces the downstream user to credit your specific component.
  • It does not force them to change the license of their own unique, proprietary add-ons or comingled work.
  • Unlike Share Alike, it only forces the downstream user to credit your specific component. It does not force them to change the license of their own unique, proprietary add-ons or comingled work.

Discussion Time

Scenario A

Your lab neighbor downloads a clean, un-licensed Python script from a public GitHub repo, fixes a minor bug, and uses it to generate the main figure for a high-impact paper.

Did your classmate commit copyright infringement? If the paper is published, is the science legally reproducible?

Class Activities

Activity 1

Consider a real-world scientific repository containing 4 distinct files:

  1. model_simulation.py (The logic script)
  2. patient_clinical_trials.csv (Raw data matrix)
  3. manuscript_draft.qmd (The text narrative)
  4. results_plot.png (The visual graph)


The Challenge: Fix a legally broken, computationally corrupted research repository.

Activity 2

Consider another project with the following components:

  1. Repo has no LICENSE file
  2. Raw data has a CC BY-NC-ND license
  3. The main script relies on a secret, proprietary tool

With the given cards, find the one that solves each issue.

Poll

If a scientific pipeline relies on an encrypted corporate file, commercial software, or sensitive dataset that legally cannot be shared, what should happen?

  1. Total Rejection: The paper should be banned from scientific journals; unshareable code is fundamentally unshareable science.

  2. Conditional Acceptance: Allow publication as long as the authors explicitly write out a text description of what the hidden code does.

  3. Partial Openness: Mandate that they open-source only the specific custom lines they wrote themselves, even if the base system remains a black box.

  4. Full Pass: Trust the authors; proprietary dependencies are a normal reality of working with industry partners.
